questions.question: The chapter's epigraph is a scholastic argument about ships and captains. Who wrote it, and what popular paraphrase does the book supply?

options.text: St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica (1265–1274) — popularly paraphrased as 'If the highest aim of a captain was to preserve his ship, he would keep it in port forever'
John Gall, Systemantics (1975) — paraphrased as 'complex systems must grow from simple ones'
Donald Knuth — paraphrased as 'premature optimization is the root of all evil'
Bruce Schneier — paraphrased as 'data is the pollution of the information age'

questions.explanation: Safety is not the highest aim — which frames a chapter about moving beyond the status quo.

questions.question: How does the author describe the shift of perspective in this final chapter?

options.text: So far the book has been mostly about describing things as they are at present; in this final chapter it shifts to discussing how things should be. Since opinions and speculation about the future are of course subjective, he adopts the first person when writing about his personal opinions
It continues describing things as they are, in the third person
It becomes purely mathematical
It summarizes the earlier chapters with no new material

questions.explanation: The author explicitly invites the reader to disagree, hoping the ideas at least form the starting point for a productive discussion and bring clarity to concepts that are often confused.

questions.question: What is the goal outlined in Chapter 1, and how did the earlier chapters serve it?

options.text: To explore how to create applications and systems that are reliable, scalable and maintainable — with fault-tolerance algorithms serving reliability, partitioning serving scalability, and evolution and abstraction serving maintainability
To catalogue every available database product
To prove impossibility results about distributed systems
To teach SQL and MapReduce

questions.explanation: The chapter brings all of these ideas together and builds on them to envisage the future.

questions.question: The opening states the goal for future applications using four adjectives. Which?

options.text: Robust, correct, evolvable, and ultimately beneficial to humanity
Fast, cheap, reliable and secure
Reliable, scalable, maintainable and observable
Robust, correct, performant and profitable

questions.explanation: 'Beneficial to humanity' is unusual for a technical book, and it sets up the closing section on Doing the Right Thing.

questions.question: What is the recurring theme the section opens with, and which chapters illustrate it?

options.text: That for any given problem there are several solutions, all of which have different pros, cons and trade-offs — as with log-structured storage, B-trees and column-oriented storage in Chapter 3, and single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication in Chapter 5
That there is always one best solution, discovered over time
That performance always dominates other concerns
That trade-offs disappear at sufficient scale

questions.explanation: 'I want to store some data and look it up again later' has no one right solution — yet an individual software implementation still has to pick one particular approach, because it's hard enough to get one code path robust and performing well, and trying to do everything in one piece of software almost guarantees that the implementation will be poor.

questions.question: Quote the chapter's claim about general-purpose databases.

options.text: Every piece of software, even a so-called 'general-purpose' database, is designed for a particular usage pattern
General-purpose databases serve every usage pattern adequately
There is no such thing as a general-purpose database
General-purpose databases are always the right default choice

questions.explanation: This sentence is load-bearing: it justifies the whole data-integration argument that follows. The first challenge is to figure out the mapping between the software products and the circumstances in which they are a good fit — and vendors are understandably reluctant to tell you about the kinds of workloads for which their software is poorly suited. Another challenge is that you often need to cobble together several different pieces of software.

questions.question: Give the chapter's opening example of tool combination, and why neither tool suffices alone.

options.text: Integrating an OLTP database with a full-text search index to handle queries for arbitrary keywords. Although some databases such as PostgreSQL have a full-text indexing feature that can be sufficient for simple applications, more sophisticated search facilities require specialist information retrieval tools — and conversely, search indexes are generally not very suitable as a durable system of record
Integrating two relational databases from different vendors
Integrating a cache with a message broker
Integrating a graph database with a key-value store

questions.explanation: As the number of different representations of the data increases, the integration problem becomes harder: besides the database and search index, there may be analytics systems such as data warehouses or batch and stream processing systems, caches or denormalized versions of objects, machine learning, classification, ranking or recommendation systems, and notifications.

questions.question: Engineers often say 'in my experience, 99% of people only need X'. What does the author say such statements reveal?

options.text: That such statements say more about the experience of the speaker than about the actual usefulness of a technology: the range of different things you might want to do with data is dizzyingly wide, and what one person considers to be an obscure and pointless feature may well be a central requirement for someone else. The need for data integration often only becomes apparent if you zoom out and consider the dataflows across an entire organization
That the 99% figure is statistically robust
That most features are genuinely unnecessary
That data integration is rarely needed

questions.explanation: When the same data is kept in several storage systems you must be very clear about the inputs and outputs: where is data written first, and which representations are derived from which sources?

questions.question: If the application writes directly to both the search index and the database, what goes wrong?

options.text: Conflicting writes may arrive in a different order at each system, so neither the database nor the search index is 'in charge' of determining the order of writes — leaving the two permanently inconsistent even though no error occurred. The missing property is a single authority on ordering
Writes are simply slower, with no correctness issue
The search index rejects the writes
The database rejects the writes

questions.explanation: This is an integrity violation, not a lag — exactly the distinction the chapter draws later between timeliness and integrity. If instead you funnel all user input through a single system that decides an ordering for all writes, it becomes much easier to derive other representations of the data by processing the writes in the same order: this is an application of state machine replication, and whether you use change data capture or an event sourcing log is less important than simply the principle of deciding on a total order.

questions.question: What two properties of event-log-based updates make fault recovery easy?

options.text: Determinism and idempotence
Atomicity and durability
Linearizability and serializability
Ordering and replication

questions.explanation: Updating a derived data system based on an event log can often be made deterministic and idempotent, making it quite easy to recover from faults.

questions.question: How do distributed transactions and log-based derived data achieve similar goals differently?

options.text: Distributed transactions decide on an ordering of writes by using locks for mutual exclusion, while CDC and event sourcing use a log for ordering. Distributed transactions use atomic commit to ensure changes take effect exactly once, while log-based systems are often based on deterministic retry and idempotence
Both use locks and atomic commit
Both use logs and idempotence
They achieve entirely unrelated goals

questions.explanation: The biggest difference is that transaction systems usually provide linearizability, which implies useful guarantees such as reading your own writes, whereas derived data systems are often updated asynchronously and so do not by default offer the same timing guarantees.

questions.question: Summarize the author's position on distributed transactions, keeping every hedge.

options.text: Within limited environments that are willing to pay the cost of distributed transactions, they have been used successfully. However, he thinks that XA has poor fault tolerance and performance characteristics, which severely limit its usefulness; he believes it might be possible to create a better protocol for distributed transactions, but getting such a protocol widely adopted and integrated with existing tools is challenging and unlikely to happen soon. So in the absence of widespread support for a good distributed transaction protocol, he believes log-based derived data is the most promising approach for integrating different data systems
Distributed transactions are always the right answer
Distributed transactions have never worked anywhere
A better protocol already exists and is widely adopted

questions.explanation: Successful in limited environments, poor in general, potentially improvable but not soon. However, he pushes back on the slogan that 'eventual consistency is inevitable — suck it up and learn to deal with it': guarantees such as reading your own writes are useful, and telling application developers to just live without them is not helpful, at least not without good guidance on how to deal with it. The middle ground is developed under Aiming for Correctness.

questions.question: Which limits on total ordering does the chapter give as systems scale? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the throughput of events is greater than a single machine can handle, you need to partition across multiple machines — but then the order of events in two different partitions is ambiguous, since constructing a totally ordered log requires all events to pass through a single leader node

If servers are spread across multiple geographically distributed datacenters, you typically have a separate leader in each datacenter, because network delays make synchronous cross-datacenter coordination inefficient — which implies an undefined ordering of events that originate in two different datacenters

When applications are deployed as microservices, a common design choice is to deploy each service and its durable state as an independent unit with no durable state shared between services — so when two events originate in different services, there is no defined order for those events
If more than one producer process appends to the same log partition, the append cannot be made atomic, so ordering within that partition is lost

questions.explanation: That last option is false — appends within a partition are ordered. The chapter's fourth genuine limit is client-side state: some applications update state immediately on user input and even continue to work offline, and with such applications clients and servers are very likely to see events in different orders. In formal terms, deciding on a total order of events is known as total order broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus — and most consensus algorithms are designed for situations in which the throughput of a single node is sufficient to process the entire stream of events, so they do not provide a mechanism for multiple nodes to share the work of ordering the events. It is still an open research problem to design consensus algorithms that can scale beyond the throughput of a single node and work well in a geographically distributed setting.

questions.question: When does a missing total order not matter?

options.text: In cases where there is no causal link between events, the lack of a total order is not a big problem, since concurrent events can be ordered arbitrarily. And some other cases are easy to handle: when there are multiple updates of the same object, they can be totally ordered by routing all updates for a particular object ID to the same log partition
Whenever the events are on the same machine
Whenever clocks are synchronized
It always matters, with no exceptions

questions.explanation: However, causal dependencies sometimes arise in more subtle ways.

questions.question: Walk the unfriend-then-complain example.

options.text: In a social networking service, two users who were in a relationship have just broken up. One of the users removes the other as a friend, and then sends a message to their remaining friends complaining about their ex-partner. The user's intention is that their ex-partner should not see the rude message, since the message was sent after the friend status was revoked. But if friendship status is stored in one place and messages in another place, that ordering dependency between the unfriend event and the message-send event may be lost — and if the causal dependency is not captured, a service that sends notifications about new messages may process the message-send event before the unfriend event, and thus incorrectly send a notification to the ex-partner
Two users concurrently send the same message and one is lost
A user's profile update arrives before their account creation
Two users unfriend each other simultaneously

questions.explanation: The notification is effectively a join between the messages and the friend list, making it an instance of the timing issues discussed for stream joins.

questions.question: What does the chapter admit before listing remedies, and what starting points does it give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The admission: unfortunately, there does not seem to be a simple answer to this problem

Logical timestamps can provide total ordering without coordination, so they may help in cases where total order broadcast is not feasible — but they still require recipients to handle events that are delivered out of order, and they require additional metadata to be passed around

If you can log an event to record the state of the system that the user saw before making a decision, and give that event a unique identifier, then any later events can reference that event identifier in order to record the causal dependency
Synchronizing all machine clocks with NTP to within a few milliseconds, which is enough to recover the causal order of events from their timestamps

questions.explanation: The clock-synchronization option is ruled out by Chapter 8. A third genuine starting point the chapter gives: conflict resolution algorithms help with processing events delivered in an unexpected order — useful for maintaining state, but they do not help if actions have external side effects, such as sending a notification to a user. Each starting point comes with a limitation. The subsection ends hopefully but hedged: perhaps, over time, patterns for application development will emerge that allow causal dependencies to be captured efficiently, and derived state to be maintained correctly, without forcing all events to go through the bottleneck of total order broadcast.

questions.question: Give the author's statement of the goal of data integration.

options.text: 'I would say that the goal of data integration is to make sure that data ends up in the right form in all the right places' — which requires consuming inputs, transforming, joining, filtering, aggregating, training models, evaluating, and eventually writing to the appropriate outputs. Batch and stream processors are the tools for achieving this goal
To store all data in a single database
To eliminate derived data entirely
To ensure all systems are linearizable

questions.explanation: Note that 'training models' sits in the same list as filtering and aggregating — machine learning is treated as just another derivation. The outputs of batch and stream processes are derived datasets such as search indexes, materialized views, recommendations to show to users, and aggregate metrics.

questions.question: What is the main fundamental difference between batch and stream processing, and what about the others?

options.text: That stream processors operate on unbounded datasets whereas batch process inputs are of a known, finite size. There are also many detailed differences in the ways the processing engines are implemented, but these distinctions are beginning to blur
That batch is deterministic and streaming is not; the other differences are permanent
That batch uses HDFS and streaming uses Kafka; nothing else differs
That streaming is always faster; the other differences are cosmetic

questions.explanation: Spark performs stream processing on top of a batch processing engine by breaking the stream into microbatches, whereas Apache Flink performs batch processing on top of a stream processing engine. In principle one type of processing can be emulated on top of the other, although the performance characteristics vary — for example microbatching may perform poorly on hopping or sliding windows.

questions.question: What functional properties does the chapter attribute to batch processing?

options.text: Batch processing has a quite strong functional flavor, even if the code is not written in a functional programming language: it encourages deterministic, pure functions whose output depends only on the input and which have no side effects other than the explicit outputs, treating inputs as immutable and outputs as append-only. Stream processing is similar, but it extends operators to allow managed, fault-tolerant state
Batch processing is inherently stateful and side-effecting
Batch processing requires a functional programming language
Batch processing has no functional properties

questions.explanation: The principle of deterministic functions with well-defined inputs and outputs is not only good for fault tolerance, it also simplifies reasoning about the dataflows in an organization: no matter whether the derived data is a search index, a statistical model, or a cache, it helps to think in terms of data pipelines that derive one thing from another, pushing state changes in one system through functional application code and applying the effects to derived systems.

questions.question: Derived data systems could be maintained synchronously. Why is asynchrony preferred?

options.text: Because asynchrony is what makes systems based on event logs robust: it allows a fault in one part of the system to be contained locally, whereas distributed transactions abort if any one participant fails, so they tend to amplify failures by spreading them to the rest of the system. In principle derived data systems could be maintained synchronously, just like a relational database updates secondary indexes synchronously within the same transaction as writes to the table being indexed
Because synchronous updates are impossible to implement
Because asynchrony is faster and that is the only reason
Because relational databases update indexes asynchronously too

questions.explanation: Fault containment, not speed, is the primary argument. A partitioned system with secondary indexes must either send writes to multiple partitions, if the index is term-partitioned, or send reads to all partitions, if it is document-partitioned — and such cross-partition communication is also most reliable and scalable if the index is maintained asynchronously.

questions.question: Which of batch and stream processing does what when maintaining derived data?

options.text: Stream processing allows changes in the input to be reflected in derived views with low delay, whereas batch processing allows large amounts of accumulated historical data to be reprocessed in order to derive new views onto an existing dataset
Batch gives low delay; streaming reprocesses history
Both only handle recent data
Both only handle historical data

questions.explanation: Without reprocessing, schema evolution is limited to simple changes like adding a new optional field to a record, or adding a new type of record — and this is the case both in a schema-on-write and in a schema-on-read context. With reprocessing it is possible to restructure a dataset into a completely different model in order to better serve new requirements.

questions.question: What does the railway-gauge box concede at the end?

options.text: That such conversions can be done gradually over the course of years — but nevertheless it is an expensive undertaking, which is why nonstandard gauges still exist today: for example the BART system in the San Francisco Bay Area uses a different gauge from the majority of the US
That gauge conversion is impossible
That all railways converged on one gauge successfully
That gauge standardization was free

questions.explanation: The moral is not that migration is easy — it is that migration is possible but so expensive that people often don't finish.

questions.question: Describe the gradual migration that derived views enable.

options.text: You do not need to perform the migration as a sudden switch: instead you can maintain the old schema and the new schema side by side as two independently derived views onto the same underlying data. Then you can start shifting a small number of users to the new view in order to test its performance and find any bugs, while most users continue to be routed to the old view — and gradually you can increase the proportion of users accessing the new view, and eventually drop the old view
You must switch all users at once after a full rewrite
You must take the system offline for the migration
You must migrate the underlying data destructively

questions.explanation: The beauty of such a gradual migration is that every stage of the process is easily reversible if something goes wrong: you always have a working system to go back to. By reducing the risk of irreversible damage, you can be more confident about going ahead, and thus move faster to improve your system.

questions.question: State the lambda architecture's core idea and its two parallel systems.

options.text: The core idea is that incoming data should be recorded by appending immutable events to an always-growing dataset, similarly to event sourcing, and from these events read-optimized views are derived. The lambda architecture proposes running two different systems in parallel: a batch processing system such as Hadoop MapReduce, and a separate stream-processing system such as Storm
One database and one cache, run in parallel
Two identical stream processors for redundancy
A single unified engine handling both batch and stream

questions.explanation: In the lambda approach the stream processor consumes the events and quickly produces an approximate update to the view, while the batch processor later consumes the same set of events and produces a corrected version of the derived view. The reasoning: batch processing is simpler and thus less prone to bugs, while stream processors are thought to be less reliable and harder to make fault-tolerant — and moreover the stream process can use fast approximate algorithms while the batch process uses slower exact algorithms.

questions.question: What does the author credit the lambda architecture with before criticizing it?

options.text: That it was an influential idea that shaped the design of data systems for the better — particularly by popularizing the principle of deriving views onto streams of immutable events and reprocessing events when needed. However, he also thinks it has a number of practical problems
Nothing; he rejects it entirely
That it is the final architecture for data systems
That it eliminated the need for batch processing

questions.explanation: Influential and directionally right, with practical problems.

questions.question: Which practical problems with the lambda architecture does the author give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Duplicated logic: having to maintain the same logic to run both in a batch and in a stream processing framework is significant additional effort — and although libraries such as Summingbird provide an abstraction for computations that can be run in either a batch or a streaming context, the operational complexity of debugging, tuning and maintaining two different systems remains

Merging two outputs: since the stream pipeline and the batch pipeline produce separate outputs, they need to be merged in order to respond to user requests. This merge is fairly easy if the computation is a simple aggregation over a tumbling window, but it becomes significantly harder if the view is derived using more complex operations such as joins and sessionization, or if the output is not a time series

Reprocessing cost forces incrementalization: although it is nice to have the ability to reprocess the entire historical dataset, doing so frequently is expensive on large datasets — so the batch pipeline often needs to be set up to process incremental batches, such as an hour's worth of data at the end of every hour, which raises the problems of handling stragglers and handling windows that cross boundaries between batches. Incrementalizing a batch computation adds complexity, making it more akin to the streaming layer, which runs counter to the goal of keeping the batch layer as simple as possible
The lambda architecture cannot express joins at all

questions.explanation: Three objections, all practical rather than conceptual.

questions.question: Which features enable the benefits of lambda without its downsides? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The ability to replay historical events through the same processing engine that handles the stream of recent events — for example log-based message brokers have the ability to replay messages, and some stream processors can read input from a distributed filesystem such as HDFS

Exactly-once semantics for stream processors, so that the output is the same as if no faults had occurred even if faults did in fact occur — which, like with batch processing, requires discarding the partial output of any failed tasks

Tools for windowing by event time, not by processing time, since processing time is meaningless when reprocessing historical events. For example Apache Beam provides an API for expressing such computations, which can then be run using Apache Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow
A second redundant batch layer for correction

questions.explanation: Three features, becoming increasingly widely available.

questions.question: 'At a most abstract level, databases, Hadoop, and operating systems all perform the same functions.' Which?

options.text: They store some data, and they allow you to process and query that data. A database stores data in records of some data model — rows in tables, documents, vertices in a graph — while an operating system's filesystem stores data in files; but at their core, both are 'information management' systems. And as Chapter 10 showed, the Hadoop ecosystem is somewhat like a distributed version of Unix
They all provide transactions and query optimization
They all provide network services
They all provide user authentication

questions.explanation: Of course, there are many practical differences: for example many filesystems do not cope very well with a directory containing 10 million small files, whereas a database containing 10 million small records is completely normal and unremarkable.

questions.question: Match Unix and relational databases to their stated purposes.

options.text: Unix viewed its purpose as presenting programmers with a logical but fairly low-level hardware abstraction, whereas relational databases wanted to give application programmers a high-level abstraction that would hide the complexities of data structures on disk, concurrency, crash recovery and so on. Unix developed pipes and files that are just sequences of bytes, whereas databases developed SQL and transactions
Unix aimed at high-level abstraction and databases at low-level hardware access
Both aimed at the same level of abstraction
Neither developed an abstraction

questions.explanation: Which approach is better? Of course, it depends what you want. Unix is 'simpler' in the sense that it is a fairly thin wrapper around hardware resources; relational databases are 'simpler' in the sense that a short declarative query can draw on a lot of powerful infrastructure — query optimization, indexes, join methods, concurrency control, replication and so on — without the author of the query needing to understand the implementation details. Both are simple, for different people.

questions.question: How long has this tension lasted, and how does the author read the NoSQL movement?

options.text: The tension has lasted for decades — both Unix and the relational model emerged in the early 1970s — and still isn't resolved. He would interpret the NoSQL movement as wanting to apply a Unix-esque approach of low-level abstractions to the domain of distributed OLTP data storage, and says he will attempt to reconcile the two philosophies in the hope that we can combine the best of both worlds
The tension was resolved in the 1980s in favour of databases
NoSQL applied the relational philosophy to new data models
The tension is new, dating from 2009

questions.explanation: Fifty years unresolved, with NoSQL as the Unix-side resurgence.

questions.question: Walk what a database does when you run CREATE INDEX.

options.text: It scans over a consistent snapshot of a table, picks out all of the field values being indexed, sorts them, and writes out the index. Then it must process the backlog of writes that have been made since the consistent snapshot was taken, assuming the table was not locked while creating the index so writes could continue. After that it must continue to keep the index up to date whenever a transaction writes to the table
It locks the table and builds the index in one pass
It rebuilds the index on every query
It stores the index in memory only

questions.explanation: Notice that this process is remarkably similar to setting up a new follower replica, and also very similar to bootstrapping change data capture in a streaming system. Whenever you run CREATE INDEX the database essentially reprocesses the existing dataset and derives the index as a new view onto the existing data — the existing data may be a snapshot of the state rather than a log of all changes that ever happened, but the two are closely related.

questions.question: State the 'meta-database of everything' claim.

options.text: That the dataflow across an entire organization starts looking like one huge database: whenever a batch, stream, or ETL process transports data from one place and form to another place and form, it is acting like the database subsystem that keeps indexes or materialized views up to date. Viewed like this, batch and stream processors are like elaborate implementations of triggers, stored procedures and materialized view maintenance routines, and the derived data systems they maintain are like different index types — just as a relational database may support B-tree indexes, hash indexes and spatial indexes, except that these are various different pieces of software, running on different machines, administered by different teams
That all organizations should use one physical database
That databases should be replaced by filesystems
That ETL processes are unnecessary

questions.explanation: Same roles, different machines and teams.

questions.question: Define the two avenues the author speculates about.

options.text: Federated databases, unifying reads: it is possible to provide a unified query interface to a wide variety of underlying storage engines and processing methods — an approach known as a federated database or polystore, as with PostgreSQL's foreign data wrapper. Applications that need a specialized data model or query interface can still access the underlying storage engines directly, while users who want to combine data from disparate places can do so easily through the federated interface. This follows the relational tradition of a single integrated system with a high-level query language and elegant semantics, but a complicated implementation. And unbundled databases, unifying writes: while federation addresses read-only querying across several different systems, it does not have a good answer to synchronizing writes across those systems. Within a single database creating a consistent index is a built-in feature; when we compose several storage systems we need to ensure that all data changes end up in all the right places, even in the face of faults — so making it easier to plug together storage systems, for example through change data capture and event logs, is like unbundling a database's index-maintenance features in a way that can synchronize writes across disparate technologies. This follows the Unix tradition of small tools that do one thing well, communicate through a uniform low-level API (pipes), and can be composed using a higher-level language (the shell)
Federation for writes and unbundling for reads
Both address reads only
Both address writes only

questions.explanation: Federation and unbundling are two sides of the same coin: composing a reliable, scalable, and maintainable system out of diverse components. Federated read-only querying requires mapping one data model into another, which takes some thought but is ultimately quite a manageable problem — the author thinks keeping the writes to several storage systems in sync is the harder engineering problem, and so focuses on it.

questions.question: What is the traditional approach to synchronizing writes, and what does the author propose instead?

options.text: The traditional approach is distributed transactions across heterogeneous storage systems — which he thinks is the wrong solution. Transactions within a single storage or stream processing system are feasible, but when data crosses the boundary between different technologies, he believes an asynchronous event log with idempotent writes is a much more robust and practical approach
The traditional approach is event logs, and he proposes distributed transactions
The traditional approach is dual writes, which he endorses
There is no traditional approach

questions.explanation: For example, distributed transactions are used within some stream processors to achieve exactly-once semantics, and this can work quite well — however, when a transaction would need to involve systems written by different groups of people, such as writing data from a stream processor to a distributed key-value store or search index, the lack of a standardized transaction protocol makes integration much harder. An ordered log of events with idempotent consumers is a much simpler abstraction, and thus much more feasible to implement across heterogeneous systems.

questions.question: At which levels does log-based integration's loose coupling manifest? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At a system level: asynchronous event streams make the system as a whole more robust to outages or performance degradation of individual components, because if a consumer runs slow or fails the event log can buffer messages, allowing the producer and any other consumers to continue running unaffected. The faulty consumer can catch up when it is fixed, so it doesn't miss any data, and the fault is contained — whereas the synchronous interaction of distributed transactions tends to escalate local faults into large-scale failures

At a human level: unbundling data systems allows different software components and services to be developed, improved, and maintained independently from each other by different teams. Specialization allows each team to focus on doing one thing well, and event streams provide an interface that is powerful enough to capture fairly strong consistency properties, due to durability and ordering of events, but also general enough to be applicable to almost any kind of data
At a hardware level, by removing the need for special networks
At a legal level, by removing liability

questions.explanation: System-level fault containment and human-level team independence.

questions.question: State the goal of unbundling, and the decision rule that follows.

options.text: The goal of unbundling is not to compete with individual databases on performance for particular workloads: the goal is to allow you to combine several different databases in order to achieve good performance for a much wider range of workloads than is possible with a single piece of software. It's about breadth, not depth. So if there is a single technology that does everything you need, you're most likely best off simply using that product rather than trying to reimplement it yourself from lower-level components — the advantages of unbundling and composition only come into the picture when there is no single piece of software that satisfies all your requirements
The goal is to beat every specialized database on its own benchmark
The goal is to eliminate all databases
The goal is depth, not breadth

questions.explanation: Breadth over depth, in the same vein as the diversity of storage and processing models discussed under comparing Hadoop to distributed databases.

questions.question: What major part does the author say is missing?

options.text: That we don't yet have the unbundled-database equivalent of the Unix shell — namely a high-level language for composing storage and processing systems in a simple and declarative way. He would love it if we could simply declare something like 'mysql pipe elasticsearch' — the unbundled equivalent of CREATE INDEX — which would take all the documents in a MySQL database and index them in an Elasticsearch cluster, then continually capture all the changes made to the database and automatically apply them to the search index, without us having to write custom application code; and it should be possible with almost any kind of storage or indexing system
A faster storage engine
A distributed transaction protocol
Nothing is missing

questions.explanation: The second wish concerns caches: it would be nice to precompute and update caches more easily, since a materialized view is essentially a precomputed cache — so it would be interesting to create a cache by declaratively specifying materialized views for complex queries, including recursive queries on graphs and application logic. There is early-stage research in this area, such as differential dataflow, and the author hopes these ideas will find their way into production systems.

questions.question: What name has this approach become known by, and how does the author qualify it?

options.text: 'Database inside-out', after the title of a conference talk he gave in 2014 — however, calling it a 'new architecture' is too grandiose: he sees it more as a design pattern, a starting point for discussion, named simply so that we can better talk about it
'Lambda architecture', which he claims as his own invention
'Kappa architecture', a proven production design
It has no name

questions.explanation: These ideas are not his: they are an amalgamation of other people's ideas from which we should learn — in particular dataflow languages such as Oz and Juttle, functional reactive programming languages such as Elm, and logic programming languages such as Bloom. The term unbundling in this context was proposed by Jay Kreps.

questions.question: What can a spreadsheet do that the chapter says is miles ahead of most programming languages?

options.text: Dataflow programming capabilities: you can put a formula in one cell, such as the sum of cells in another column, and whenever any input to the formula changes, the result of the formula is automatically recalculated. This is exactly what we want at a data system level: when a record in a database changes, we want any index for that record to be automatically updated, and any cached views or aggregations that depend on the record to be automatically refreshed — and you should not have to worry about the technical details of how this refresh happens, but be able to simply trust that it works correctly
Type checking across cells
Transactional isolation between cells
Distributed execution across machines

questions.explanation: Automatic recalculation on input change is the model the chapter wants for derived data.

questions.question: Give the derivation functions for a secondary index and a full-text search index.

options.text: A secondary index is a straightforward transformation function: for each row or document in the base table it picks out the values in the columns or fields being indexed, and sorts by those values — assuming a B-tree or SSTable index, which are sorted by key. A full-text search index is created by applying various natural language processing functions such as language detection, word segmentation, stemming or lemmatization, spelling correction, and synonym identification, followed by building a data structure for efficient lookups such as an inverted index
Both apply natural language processing
Both are simple sorts with no processing
Neither is a derivation function

questions.explanation: For a machine learning system you can consider the model as being derived from the training data through the application of various feature extraction and statistical analysis functions — and when the model is applied to new input data, the output of the model is derived from the input and the model, and hence indirectly from the training data. A cache often contains an aggregation of data in the form in which it is going to be displayed in a user interface, so populating the cache requires knowledge of what fields are referenced in the UI, and changes in the UI may require updating the definition of how the cache is populated and rebuilding the cache.

questions.question: Which derivation functions are built into databases, and which are not?

options.text: The derivation function for a secondary index is so commonly required that it is built into many databases as a core feature. For full-text indexing, basic linguistic features for common languages may be built into a database, but the more sophisticated features often require domain-specific tuning. In machine learning, feature engineering is notoriously application-specific, often having to incorporate detailed knowledge of the user interaction and deployment of an application — so when someone creates such a derived dataset it is unlikely that a standard cookie-cutter function will do the trick, and custom code is required. And this custom code is where many databases struggle: although relational databases commonly support triggers, stored procedures and user-defined functions, which can be used to execute application code within the database, they have been somewhat of an afterthought in database design
All derivation functions are built in
None are built in; all require custom code
Only machine learning is built in

questions.explanation: In theory, databases could be deployment environments for arbitrary application code, like an operating system — however in practice they have turned out to be poorly suited for this purpose, because they don't fit well with the requirements of modern application development such as dependency and package management, version control, rolling upgrades, evolvability, monitoring, metrics, calls to network services, and integration with external systems.

questions.question: Which tools does the chapter name for running application code, and what is the argument?

options.text: Deployment and cluster management tools such as Mesos, YARN, Docker, Kubernetes and others, which are designed specifically for the purpose of running application code. By focusing on doing one thing well, they are able to do it much better than a database that provides execution of user-defined functions as one of its many features. The conclusion: it probably makes sense to have some parts of a system that specialize in durable data storage, and other parts that specialize in running application code — the two can interact while still remaining independent
Only stored procedures, which are preferable
Only PostgreSQL extensions
No tools exist for this purpose

questions.explanation: Specialization beats a database's user-defined-function feature.

questions.question: Describe the stateless-service deployment model and the joke the chapter quotes.

options.text: Most web applications today are deployed as stateless services, in which any user request can be routed to any application server and the server forgets everything about the request once it has sent the response. This style of deployment is convenient, as servers can be added or removed at will — but the state has to go somewhere: typically a database. The trend is to keep stateless application logic separate from state management (databases): not putting application logic in the database and not putting persistent state in the application. As people in the functional programming community like to joke, 'We believe in the separation of Church and state' — and a footnote explains: Church here is a reference to Alonzo Church, who created the lambda calculus, which has no mutable state, so one could say that mutable state is separate from Church's work
Applications are stateful and databases stateless; the joke is about religion
State is kept in the application; the joke is about Alan Turing
There is no such trend and no joke

questions.explanation: In this typical web application model the database acts as a kind of mutable shared variable that can be accessed synchronously over the network: the application can read and update the variable, and the database takes care of making it durable, providing some concurrency control and fault tolerance.

questions.question: What can you not do with a mutable variable, and what did databases inherit?

options.text: In most programming languages you cannot subscribe to changes in a mutable variable — you can only read it periodically. Unlike in a spreadsheet, readers of the variable don't get notified if the value of the variable changes. You can implement such subscriptions in your own code with the observer pattern, but most languages do not have this pattern as a built-in feature. Databases have inherited this passive approach to mutable data: if you want to find out whether the content of the database has changed, often your only option is to poll. Subscribing to changes is only just beginning to emerge as a feature
You cannot read a mutable variable; databases inherited that too
You can subscribe freely, and databases support it universally
Mutable variables are notified automatically in most languages

questions.explanation: Polling as the only option is the inherited limitation.

questions.question: What does thinking in terms of dataflow renegotiate?

options.text: The relationship between application code and state management. Instead of treating a database as a passive variable that is manipulated by the application, we think much more about the interplay and collaboration between state, state changes, and code that processes them — application code responds to state changes in one place by triggering state changes in another place
The relationship between clients and servers only
The relationship between disks and memory
Nothing; dataflow is only about performance

questions.explanation: Precedents: Chapter 11 discussed treating the log of changes to a database as a stream of events we can subscribe to; message-passing systems such as actors also have this concept of responding to events; and already in the 1980s the tuple spaces model explored expressing distributed computations in terms of processes that observe state changes and react to them. Similar things happen inside a database when a trigger fires due to a data change, or when a secondary index is updated to reflect a change in the table being indexed.

questions.question: Why is maintaining derived data not the same as asynchronous job execution? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Order matters: as we saw in the case of event logs and databases, the order of state changes is often important — if several consumers generate derived state or output event streams, they need to process the events in the same order so that they remain consistent with each other. Many message brokers do not have this property when redelivering unacknowledged messages, and dual writes are also ruled out

Fault tolerance is key: losing just a single message causes the derived dataset to go permanently out of sync with its data source, so both message delivery and derived state updates must be reliable. For example, many actor systems by default maintain actor state and messages in memory, so they are lost if the machine running the actor crashes
Derived data requires exactly-once delivery whereas jobs require at-most-once
There is no difference; the two are the same problem

questions.explanation: Note the word 'permanently' — a single lost message is an integrity violation, not a delay. Stable message ordering and fault-tolerant message processing are quite stringent demands, but they are much less expensive and more operationally robust than distributed transactions; and modern stream processors can provide these guarantees at scale while allowing application code to be run as stream operators, doing the arbitrary processing that built-in derivation functions in databases generally don't provide. Like Unix tools, stream operators can be composed to build large systems around dataflow, each taking streams of state changes as input and producing other streams of state changes as output.

questions.question: What does the chapter identify as the primary advantage of a service-oriented architecture?

options.text: Organizational scalability through loose coupling: different teams can work on different services, which reduces coordination effort between them — as long as the services can be deployed and updated independently
Technical performance through smaller processes
Reduced hardware cost
Stronger consistency guarantees

questions.explanation: The advantage is organizational, not technical, and it is conditional on independent deployability. Composing stream operators into dataflow systems has a lot of similar characteristics to the microservices approach — however, the underlying communication mechanism is very different: one-directional, asynchronous message streams rather than synchronous request/response interactions.

questions.question: Give both implementations of the currency conversion example.

options.text: In the microservices approach, the code that processes the purchase would probably query an exchange-rate service or database in order to obtain the current rate for a particular currency. In the dataflow approach, the code that processes purchases would subscribe to a stream of exchange rate updates ahead of time, and record the current rate in a local database whenever it changes — then when it comes to processing the purchase, it only needs to query the local database. So a synchronous network request to another service has been replaced with a query to a local database, which may be on the same machine, even in the same process
Both query a remote exchange-rate service
Both maintain a local database
The dataflow approach polls the service more frequently

questions.explanation: Not only is the dataflow approach faster, but it is also more robust to the failure of another service — the fastest and most reliable network request is no network request at all. Instead of RPC, we now have a stream join between purchase events and exchange rate update events. A footnote concedes that you could avoid the synchronous network request by caching the exchange rate locally — however, in order to keep that cache fresh you would need to periodically poll for updated exchange rates, or subscribe to a stream of changes, which is exactly what happens in the dataflow approach.

questions.question: Why is this join time-dependent, and does either design escape it?

options.text: Because if the purchase events are reprocessed at a later point in time, the exchange rate will have changed — so if you want to reconstruct the original output, you will need to obtain the historical exchange rate at the original time of purchase. And no matter whether you query a service or subscribe to a stream of exchange rate updates, you will need to handle this time dependence
Only the dataflow design suffers the time dependence
Only the microservices design suffers it
Neither design suffers it

questions.explanation: Crucially, neither design escapes it. The section ends: subscribing to a stream of changes, rather than querying the current state when needed, brings us closer to a spreadsheet-like model of computation — when some piece of data changes, any derived data that depends on it can swiftly be updated. There are still many open questions, for example around issues like time-dependent joins, but the author believes that building applications around dataflow ideas is a very promising direction to go in.

questions.question: Define the write path and the read path.

options.text: The write path is the process for creating derived datasets — search indexes, materialized views and predictive models — and keeping them up to date: whenever some piece of information is written to the system, it may go through multiple stages of batch and stream processing, and eventually every derived dataset is updated to incorporate the data that was written. The read path is what happens when serving a user request: you read from the derived dataset, perhaps perform some more processing on the results, and construct the response to the user
The write path is the network hop and the read path is the disk seek
The write path is synchronous and the read path is asynchronous by definition
They are the same path traversed in opposite directions

questions.explanation: Figure 12-1 is captioned: in a search index, writes (document updates) meet reads (queries). Taken together, the write path and the read path encompass the whole journey of the data, from the point where it is collected to the point where it is consumed, probably by another human: the write path is the portion that is precomputed, done eagerly as soon as the data comes in regardless of whether anyone has asked to see it, and the read path is the portion that only happens when someone asks for it. If you are familiar with functional programming languages, the write path is similar to eager evaluation and the read path is similar to lazy evaluation.

questions.question: What work do reads and writes each do with a full-text index, and what happens with no index?

options.text: The write path updates the index and the read path searches the index for keywords, so both need to do some work: writes need to update the index entries for all terms that appear in the document, and reads need to search for each of the words in the query and apply Boolean logic to find documents that contain all of the words (an AND operator) or any synonym of each of the words (an OR operator). Without an index, a search query would have to scan over all documents, like grep, which would get very expensive with a large number of documents — so no index means less work on the write path, since there is no index to update, but a lot more work on the read path
Only writes do work; reads are free with an index
Only reads do work; writes are free
Neither path does work with an index

questions.explanation: The opposite extreme would be precomputing the search results for all possible queries: then reads would have less to do — no Boolean logic, just find the results for your query and return them — but the write path would be a lot more expensive, since the set of possible search queries that could be asked is infinite, and thus precomputing all possible results would require infinite time and storage space. A footnote sharpens this: the set of distinct search queries with nonempty search results is finite, assuming a finite corpus — however it would be exponential in the number of terms in the corpus, which is still pretty bad news.

questions.question: Describe the intermediate design and its two names.

options.text: Precomputing the search results for only a fixed set of the most common queries, so that they can be served quickly without having to go to the index, while uncommon queries can still be served from the index. This would generally be called a cache of common queries, although we could also call it a materialized view, as it would need to be updated when new documents appear that should be included in the results of one of the common queries
Precomputing all queries, called a materialized view
Precomputing no queries, called a cache
There is no intermediate design

questions.explanation: An index is not the only possible boundary between the write path and the read path. Viewed like this, the role of caches, indexes and materialized views is simple: they shift the boundary between the read path and the write path, allowing us to do more work on the write path by precomputing results in order to save effort on the read path.

questions.question: Which earlier example in the book was about shifting this boundary?

options.text: The Twitter example at the beginning of the book, under Describing Load — including the wrinkle that the boundary between write path and read path might be drawn differently for celebrities compared to ordinary users. As the chapter puts it: after 500 pages we have come full circle
The MapReduce log analysis example
The shopping cart example
The doctors-on-call example

questions.explanation: The author finds the idea of a boundary between write and read paths interesting because we can discuss shifting that boundary and explore what that shift means in practical terms. The assumption he then questions: the client/server model — in which clients are largely stateless and servers have the authority over data — is so common that we almost forget that anything else exists; however technology keeps moving on, and he thinks it is important to question the status quo from time to time.

questions.question: What used to be about the only thing you could do offline in a browser, and what changed?

options.text: Just about the only thing you could do offline was to scroll up and down in a page that you had previously loaded while online. However, recent 'single-page' JavaScript web apps have gained a lot of stateful capabilities, including client-side user interface interaction and persistent local storage in the web browser — and mobile apps can similarly store a lot of state on the device and don't require a round-trip to the server for most user interactions
Nothing changed; browsers remain stateless
Browsers gained transactions and SQL
Browsers gained server-side rendering

questions.explanation: These changing capabilities have led to renewed interest in offline-first applications that do as much as possible using a local database on the same device, without requiring an internet connection, and sync with remote servers in the background when a network connection is available — since mobile devices often have slow and unreliable cellular internet connections, it's a big advantage for users if their user interface does not have to wait for synchronous network requests, and if apps mostly work offline.

questions.question: When state lives on end-user devices, how does the chapter re-describe the layers?

options.text: We can think of the on-device state as a cache of state on the server: the pixels on the screen are a materialized view onto model objects in the client app, and the model objects are a local replica of state in a remote datacenter
The screen is the system of record and the datacenter a cache of it
The model objects are the only authoritative state
There is no relationship between the layers

questions.explanation: Two levels of derivation, from datacenter to device to pixels.

questions.question: Why doesn't a loaded web page notice server-side changes, and what is RSS really?

options.text: Because if the data subsequently changes on the server, the browser does not find out about the change until you reload the page: the browser only reads the data at one point in time, assuming that it is static — it does not subscribe to updates from the server. Thus the state on the device is a stale cache that is not updated unless you explicitly poll for changes. And HTTP-based feed subscription protocols like RSS are really just a basic form of polling
Because browsers cannot open TCP connections; RSS is a push protocol
Because servers cannot track clients; RSS is a WebSocket protocol
Browsers do notice changes automatically

questions.explanation: More recent protocols have moved beyond the basic request/response pattern of HTTP: server-sent events (the EventSource API) and WebSockets provide communication channels by which a web browser can keep an open TCP connection to a server, and the server can actively push messages to the browser as long as it remains connected — giving the server an opportunity to actively inform the end-user client about any changes to the state it has stored locally, reducing the staleness of the client-side state.

questions.question: In write-path/read-path terms, what does pushing state changes to devices amount to?

options.text: Extending the write path all the way to the end user. When a client is first initialized it would still need to use a read path to get its initial state, but thereafter it could rely on a stream of state changes sent by the server. The ideas around stream processing and messaging are not restricted to running only in a datacenter: we can take them further and extend them all the way to end-user devices
Extending the read path to the server
Eliminating both paths
Replacing the write path with polling

questions.explanation: Devices will be offline sometimes and unable to receive notifications — but we already solved that problem: consumer offsets let a consumer of a log-based message broker reconnect after failing or becoming disconnected and ensure it doesn't miss any messages that arrived while it was disconnected. The same technique works for individual users, where each device is a small subscriber to a small stream of events.

questions.question: Which client-side tools does the chapter name, and what resemblance does it point out?

options.text: The Elm language and Facebook's toolchain of React, Flux and Redux already manage internal client-side state by subscribing to a stream of events representing user input or responses from a server, structured similarly to event sourcing
Angular and Vue, which use polling
jQuery and Backbone, which use request/response
No client-side tools resemble event sourcing

questions.explanation: The challenge: the assumption of stateless clients and request/response interactions is very deeply ingrained in our databases, libraries, frameworks and protocols — many datastores support read and write operations where a request returns one response, but much fewer provide an ability to subscribe to changes, that is a request that returns a stream of responses over time. Extending write paths all the way to end users would require fundamentally rethinking the way we build many of these systems, moving away from request/response interaction and toward publish/subscribe dataflow — but the author thinks the advantages of more responsive user interfaces and better offline support would make it worth the effort, and hopes that if you are designing data systems you will keep in mind the option of subscribing to changes, not just querying the current state.

questions.question: What does the store give you that the event log alone doesn't?

options.text: The store acts as the boundary between the write path and the read path: it allows random-access read queries to the data that would otherwise require scanning the whole event log. Additionally, stream processors also need to maintain state to perform aggregations and joins — this state is normally hidden inside the stream processor, but some frameworks allow it to also be queried by outside clients, turning the stream processor itself into a kind of simple database
The store provides ordering, which the log lacks
The store provides durability, which the log lacks
The store provides nothing extra

questions.explanation: Random access without scanning is the store's contribution.

questions.question: What design does the chapter propose for reads?

options.text: So far we have assumed that writes to the store go through an event log while reads are transient network requests that go directly to the nodes that store the data being queried. This is a reasonable design, but not the only possible one: it is also possible to represent read requests as streams of events, and send both the read events and the write events through a stream processor, with the processor responding to read events by emitting the result of the read to an output stream
That reads should bypass the log entirely and always will
That reads should be batched nightly
That reads should be eliminated

questions.explanation: When both the writes and the reads are represented as events, and routed to the same stream operator in order to be handled, we are in fact performing a stream-table join between the stream of read queries and the database — so the read event needs to be sent to the database partition holding the data, just like batch and stream processors need to copartition inputs on the same key when joining.

questions.question: How do a one-off read and a subscribe differ, seen as joins?

options.text: A one-off read request just passes the request through the join operator and then immediately forgets it, whereas a subscribe request is a persistent join with past and future events on the other side of the join
Both are persistent joins
Both are transient joins
Neither is a join

questions.explanation: The chapter calls this correspondence between serving requests and performing joins quite fundamental.

questions.question: What does recording a log of read events buy you?

options.text: It has benefits with regard to tracking causal dependencies and data provenance across a system: it would allow you to reconstruct what the user saw before they made a particular decision. For example in an online shop, it is likely that the predicted shipping date and the inventory status shown to a customer affect whether they choose to buy an item — so to analyze this connection you need to record the result of the user's query of the shipping and inventory status
It reduces storage requirements
It speeds up the read path
It has no benefits

questions.explanation: Writing read events to durable storage thus enables better tracking of causal dependencies, but it incurs additional storage and I/O cost — optimizing such systems to reduce the overhead is still an open research problem. But if you already log read requests for operational purposes, as a side effect of request processing, it is not such a great change to make the log the source of the requests instead.

questions.question: When is reads-as-events overkill, and what does it open up?

options.text: For queries that only touch a single partition, the effort of sending queries through a stream and collecting a stream of responses is perhaps overkill. However, this idea opens the possibility of distributed execution of complex queries that need to combine data from several partitions, taking advantage of the infrastructure for message routing, partitioning and joining that is already provided by stream processors
It is never overkill and opens nothing new
It is always overkill
It is overkill for multi-partition queries only

questions.explanation: Storm's distributed RPC feature supports this usage pattern: it has been used to compute the number of people who have seen a URL on Twitter — the union of the follower sets of everyone who has tweeted that URL — and since the set of Twitter users is partitioned, this computation requires combining results from many partitions.

questions.question: Walk the fraud-prevention example.

options.text: A similar pattern occurs if you need to perform fraud prevention: in order to assess the risk of whether a particular purchase event is fraudulent, you can examine the reputation scores of the user's IP address, email address, billing address, shipping address and so on. Each of these reputation databases is itself partitioned, and so collecting the scores for a particular purchase event requires a sequence of joins with differently partitioned datasets
A single join against one partitioned database suffices
All reputation data is stored in one partition
Fraud prevention requires no joins

questions.explanation: The internal query execution graphs of MPP databases have similar characteristics. The honest recommendation: if you need to perform this kind of multi-partition join, it is probably simpler to use a database that provides this feature than to implement it using a stream processor — however, treating queries as streams provides an option for implementing large-scale applications that run against the limits of conventional off-the-shelf solutions.

questions.question: Why do stateful systems need more careful thought than stateless ones?

options.text: With stateless services that only read data it is no big deal if something goes wrong: you can fix the bug and restart the service, and everything returns to normal. Stateful systems such as databases are not so simple: they are designed to remember things forever, more or less, so if something goes wrong the effects also potentially last forever — which means they require more careful thought
Because stateful systems are slower
Because stateful systems are harder to deploy
There is no difference

questions.explanation: Permanent effects demand more care. Transactions have been the tool of choice for four decades for building applications that are reliable and correct — programs whose semantics are well defined and understood, even in the face of various faults. Yet the foundations are weaker than they seem: in some areas transactions are being abandoned entirely and replaced with models that offer better performance and scalability but much messier semantics, as with weak isolation levels and leaderless replication.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about our engineering methods here?

options.text: That for a topic that is so important, our understanding and our engineering methods are surprisingly flaky: it is very difficult to determine whether it is safe to run a particular application at a particular transaction isolation level or replication configuration, and often simple solutions appear to work correctly when concurrency is low and there are no faults, but turn out to have many subtle bugs in more demanding circumstances
That our methods are rigorous and well understood
That formal verification has solved the problem
That the problem is purely theoretical

questions.explanation: Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen experiments have highlighted the stark discrepancies between some products' claimed safety guarantees and their actual behavior in the presence of network problems and crashes. Even if infrastructure products like databases were free from problems, application code would still need to correctly use the features they provide, which is error-prone if the configuration is hard to understand — as is the case with weak isolation levels, quorum configurations and so on.

questions.question: What are your options, and what do serializability and atomic commit cost?

options.text: If your application can tolerate occasionally corrupting or losing data in unpredictable ways, life is a lot simpler, and you might be able to get away with simply crossing your fingers and hoping for the best. Otherwise serializability and atomic commit are established approaches, but they come at a cost: they typically only work in a single datacenter, ruling out geographically distributed architectures, and they limit the scale and fault-tolerance properties you can achieve
They cost nothing and work at any scale
They cost only money, not architecture
There are no established approaches

questions.explanation: The author's framing: while the traditional transaction approach is not going away, he also believes it is not the last word in making applications correct and resilient to faults. Transactions are not obsolete and not sufficient.

questions.question: State the thesis of 'The End-to-End Argument for Databases'.

options.text: Just because an application uses a data system that provides comparatively strong safety properties, such as serializable transactions, that does not mean the application is guaranteed to be free from data loss or corruption. For example, if an application has a bug that causes it to write incorrect data, or delete data from a database, serializable transactions aren't going to save you. This might seem like a frivolous point, but it is vitally important: application bugs occur, and people make mistakes
That serializable transactions guarantee application correctness
That immutability alone solves all correctness problems
That application bugs are rare enough to ignore

questions.explanation: The author used this fact to argue in favor of immutable and append-only data, because it is easier to recover from such mistakes if you remove the ability of faulty code to destroy good data — but although immutability is useful, it is not a cure-all by itself.

questions.question: Restate the fork in the road when message processing goes wrong, and define exactly-once.

options.text: If something goes wrong while processing a message, you can either give up — drop the message, incurring data loss — or try again. If you try again, there is the risk that it actually succeeded the first time but you just didn't find out about the success, and so the message ends up being processed twice. Processing twice is a form of data corruption: it is undesirable to charge a customer twice for the same service, billing them too much, or to increment a counter twice, overstating some metric. In this context, exactly-once means arranging the computation such that the final effect is the same as if no faults had occurred, even if the operation actually was retried due to some fault
You can only give up; retrying is forbidden
Processing twice is harmless and not corruption
Exactly-once means the message is transmitted only once

questions.explanation: The chapter also calls it effectively-once. One of the most effective approaches is to make the operation idempotent — to ensure that it has the same effect no matter whether it is executed once or multiple times. However, taking an operation that is not naturally idempotent and making it idempotent requires some effort and care: you may need to maintain some additional metadata, such as the set of operation IDs that have updated a value, and ensure fencing when failing over from one node to another.

questions.question: What does TCP use sequence numbers for, and what is the scope limitation?

options.text: TCP uses sequence numbers on packets to put them in the correct order at the recipient, and to determine whether any packets were lost or duplicated on the network: any lost packets are retransmitted and any duplicates are removed by the TCP stack before it hands the data to an application. However, this duplicate suppression only works within the context of a single TCP connection
It works across all connections between the same hosts
It works for the lifetime of the application
TCP does not suppress duplicates

questions.explanation: One connection is the entire scope — which is what makes higher-level duplicates possible.

questions.question: In the money-transfer example, what is the failure window and what happens on retry?

options.text: In many databases a transaction is tied to a client connection: if the client sends several queries, the database knows they belong to the same transaction because they are sent on the same TCP connection. If the client suffers a network interruption and connection timeout after sending the COMMIT but before hearing back from the database server, it does not know whether the transaction has been committed or aborted. On retry, the +$11.00 and −$11.00 changes are applied a second time — but now this is outside of the scope of TCP duplicate suppression, and since the transaction is not idempotent, it could happen that $22 is transferred instead of the desired $11. Thus even though this is a standard example for transaction atomicity, it is actually not correct, and real banks do not work like this
TCP duplicate suppression prevents the retry from taking effect
The database detects the duplicate transaction automatically
The retry is harmless because the transaction is idempotent

questions.explanation: The textbook atomicity example is itself not correct at the end-to-end level.

questions.question: Does two-phase commit fix this?

options.text: Two-phase commit protocols break the 1:1 mapping between a TCP connection and a transaction, since they must allow a transaction coordinator to reconnect to a database after a network fault and tell it whether to commit or abort an in-doubt transaction. Is this sufficient to ensure the transaction will only be executed once? Unfortunately not: even if we can suppress duplicate transactions between the database client and server, we still need to worry about the network between the end-user device and the application server
Yes, 2PC fully solves the duplicate problem
2PC makes the problem worse
2PC does not change the connection/transaction mapping

questions.explanation: For example, if the end-user client is a web browser it probably uses an HTTP POST request to submit an instruction to the server. Perhaps the user is on a weak cellular data connection and succeeds in sending the POST, but the signal becomes too weak before they can receive the response — in which case they will probably be shown an error message and may retry manually. Web browsers warn 'Are you sure you want to submit this form again?' and the user says yes, because they wanted the operation to happen. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern avoids this warning in normal operation, but it doesn't help if the POST request times out — and from the web server's point of view the retry is a separate request, while from the database's point of view it is a separate transaction, so the usual deduplication mechanisms don't help.

questions.question: What does making the operation idempotent through several network hops require?

options.text: It is not sufficient to rely just on a transaction mechanism provided by a database — you need to consider the end-to-end flow of the request. For example you could generate a unique identifier for an operation, such as a UUID, and include it as a hidden form field in the client application, or calculate a hash of all the relevant form fields to derive the operation ID.
