It started with the observation that there is no one single tool that can efficiently serve all possible use cases, and so applications necessarily need to compose several different pieces of software to accomplish their goals — and it discussed how to solve this data integration problem by using batch processing and event streams to let data changes flow between different systems
As a purely objective survey of existing products
As a formal treatment of consensus algorithms
As a summary of Chapters 1 through 11 with no new content

questions.explanation: In this approach, certain systems are designated as systems of record and other data is derived from them through transformations — in this way we can maintain indexes, materialized views, machine learning models, statistical summaries and more. By making these derivations and transformations asynchronous and loosely coupled, a problem in one area is prevented from spreading to unrelated parts of the system, increasing the robustness and fault-tolerance of the system as a whole.

questions.question: Give the Summary's evolution and recovery benefits of expressing dataflows as transformations.

options.text: If you want to change one of the processing steps — for example to change the structure of an index or cache — you can just rerun the new transformation code on the whole input dataset in order to rederive the output. Similarly, if something goes wrong, you can fix the code and reprocess the data in order to recover
You can only add new steps, never change existing ones
Recovery requires restoring from backup
No evolution benefits are claimed

questions.explanation: These processes are quite similar to what databases already do internally, so the chapter recast the idea of dataflow applications as unbundling the components of a database, and building an application by composing these loosely coupled components. Derived state can be updated by observing changes in the underlying data, and moreover the derived state itself can further be observed by downstream consumers — we can even take this dataflow all the way through to the end-user device that is displaying the data, and thus build user interfaces that dynamically update to reflect data changes and continue to work offline.

questions.question: Reproduce the Summary's compression of the correctness discussion.

options.text: That strong integrity guarantees can be implemented scalably with asynchronous event processing, by using end-to-end operation identifiers to make operations idempotent and by checking constraints asynchronously. Clients can either wait until the check has passed, or go ahead without waiting but risk having to apologize about a constraint violation. This approach is much more scalable and robust than the traditional approach of using distributed transactions, and fits with how many business processes work in practice
That only distributed transactions can provide integrity
That integrity must be sacrificed for scale
That clients must always wait for the constraint check

questions.explanation: By structuring applications around dataflow and checking constraints asynchronously, we can avoid most coordination and create systems that maintain integrity but still perform well, even in geographically distributed scenarios and in the presence of faults. We can then use audits to verify the integrity of data and detect corruption. Note the careful wording: avoid most coordination, not all.

questions.question: Which harms does the Summary name? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Making justifying decisions that seriously affect people's lives, and are difficult to appeal against
Leading to discrimination and exploitation
Normalizing surveillance and exposing intimate information
Higher infrastructure costs and slower software

questions.explanation: Cost and latency are not among them; the remaining harms it names are data breaches, and well-intentioned uses of data having unintended consequences — six harms in one sentence. The chapter — and the body of the book — ends: as software and data are having such a large impact on the world, we engineers must remember that we carry a responsibility to work toward the kind of world that we want to live in: a world that treats people with humanity and respect. 'I hope that we can work together toward that goal.'

questions.question: Compress Chapter 12 into its single argument.

options.text: No one tool serves every use case, so designate a system of record and derive everything else from it through asynchronous, loosely coupled transformations rather than distributed transactions; take the end-to-end argument seriously by passing operation identifiers through the whole flow and checking constraints asynchronously; use audits to verify rather than trust; and remember that the data is about people
Use a single distributed database with serializable transactions everywhere
Abandon derived data in favour of synchronous updates
Optimize for performance above correctness and ethics

questions.explanation: Derived data plus end-to-end correctness plus verification plus responsibility. Using only what this chapter says, the book has been for three things: that there is no universal tool, since there is no one single tool that can efficiently serve all possible use cases; that the hard problems are the distributed ones and they have known shapes, so you cannot just use a distributed transaction; and that derived data is the unifying idea — all in service of a world that treats people with humanity and respect.
